name: Default effect
statement: The option that takes effect when nobody acts is chosen far more often than the same option is chosen freely, and 58 studies pool to d = 0.68.
meaning: A default is whatever happens to a person who does nothing. Choice architects set one whenever a form has a pre-ticked box, a pension plan enrols new hires automatically, or a utility assigns a tariff. The claim is that moving the default moves the distribution of choices, without removing any option and without changing any price. Three routes are usually offered for why. Accepting the default costs no effort, the default tells the chooser what the institution thinks it should be, and the default becomes the reference point against which the alternatives look like losses. Which route dominates matters for policy, because effort can be engineered away and endorsement cannot. Defaults are the operational half of status quo bias, and the organ-donation evidence that made them famous sits in that entry rather than this one.

origin.who: Eric J. Johnson, John C. Hershey, Jacqueline Meszaros and Howard Kunreuther
origin.note: Their study of car insurance in two neighbouring states, where New Jersey made limited tort the default and Pennsylvania made full tort the default, is the natural experiment the default literature was built on. The article is paywalled and the figures quoted on this page were read off Dhingra and colleagues' 2012 description of it, not off the article.

evidence: The quantitative core is a meta-analysis. Jachimowicz, Duncan, Weber and Johnson searched the literature and pooled 58 datasets from 55 studies in 35 articles, with a pooled n of 73,675. The base model gives d = 0.68, 95% CI [0.53, 0.83]; a three-level model that allows for datasets nested in studies gives d = 0.63, 95% CI [0.47, 0.80]. For the binary outcomes, which are most of them, Cramér's V is 0.29, 95% CI [0.21, 0.37], and the absolute difference in take-up between default conditions averages 27.24 percentage points. Two domain moderators come out: consumer settings b = 0.73, SE = 0.23, p = 0.003, and environmental settings b = -0.47, SE = 0.27, p = 0.08. Of the three proposed routes, two moderate the effect and one does not. Endorsement gives b = 0.32, SE = 0.15, p = 0.038 and endowment b = 0.31, SE = 0.15, p = 0.044, while ease gives b = -0.05, SE = 0.15, p = 0.75. The field evidence is larger than the laboratory evidence in every sense. Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian and Metrick studied a firm that briefly required new hires to state a 401(k) decision rather than leaving non-enrolment as the default. Three months after hire, 69 percent of the active-decision cohort had enrolled against 41 percent of the standard-enrolment cohort, a gap of 28 percentage points, and the savings distribution reached at three months would have taken thirty months to reach under the ordinary default. Liebe, Gewinner and Diekmann report two Swiss field studies covering over 200,000 households and 8,000 enterprises whose supplier made renewable electricity the standard package. Around 80 percent of customers in both sectors stayed with the green default, and the effect was stable over at least four years. Electricity consumption had only a weak effect on acceptance, and accepting the default did not raise consumption afterwards.

replication.headline: Fifty-eight default studies pool to d = 0.68, and the spread around that figure is wider than the figure.
replication.detail: Jachimowicz and colleagues found the effect in the large majority of the studies they collected, and their pooled estimate is d = 0.68, 95% CI [0.53, 0.83]. Their own tests for a missing-studies problem point the other way from the usual worry. Egger's test is flat, t(56) = -0.39, p = 0.69, and trim-and-fill adds eight hypothetical studies and raises the estimate to d = 0.80, 95% CI [0.65, 0.96]. What the pooled figure conceals is heterogeneity of I-squared = 98.21 percent, falling to 92.32 percent once the three channels are entered as moderators. Most default studies find positive effects, several find nothing, and two find effects in the wrong direction. The field record is consistent with a real and large effect. DellaVigna and Linos excluded default interventions from the main sample of their nudge-unit study because defaults were rare there, only two arms of one trial out of 126. Those two arms covered 1.3 million people and moved take-up by 9.4 and 11.2 percentage points, against an average of 1.4 percentage points across the 243 nudges they did analyse.

study.cite: Jachimowicz, J. M., Duncan, S., Weber, E. U., & Johnson, E. J. (2019). When and why defaults influence decisions: A meta-analysis of default effects. Behavioural Public Policy, 3(2), 159-186.

limits: Defaults fail in the field, and the failures are informative. Bronchetti, Dee, Huffman and Magenheim ran a field experiment with 259 low-income tax filers in which part of the federal refund went into savings bonds unless the filer chose otherwise. Take-up in the control condition was about 9 percent, the default moved nothing, and the interval around the estimate rules out an effect larger than roughly 8 percentage points. Their reading is that these filers arrived with plans for the money. The meta-analytic moderator points the same way for environmental settings, where the coefficient is negative. Persistence is a separate question from take-up. Even in Carroll and colleagues' firm the enrolment gap fell to 17 percentage points at 24 months of tenure and 5 points at 42 months. Choukhmane, using more than 100 US retirement plans and a British panel, reproduces the twelve-month effect of automatic enrolment and finds it attenuated by 36 months, with modest average increases in saving at that horizon and a fitted switching cost of about $250. Almost none of this literature is preregistered multi-site replication of a single protocol. The evidence is a large number of one-off studies in different domains, which is what the 98 percent heterogeneity is measuring.
misreadings: The first error is importing the nudge literature's publication-bias problem wholesale. Mertens, Herberz, Hahnel and Brosch meta-analysed choice-architecture studies broadly, 440 effect sizes and n = 2,148,439 after their 2022 correction, and reported d = 0.43, 95% CI [0.38, 0.48]. Maier, Bartoš, Stanley, Shanks, Harris and Wagenmakers re-analysed those data with a model that allows for selective publication and got d = 0.04, 95% CI [0.00, 0.14], with d = 0.11, 95% CI [0.00, 0.24] using only the most precise estimate per study. For the decision-structure category, which is where defaults sit, they report d = 0.12 with a Bayes factor of 1.12, which is the value that decides nothing. Defaults were not the target of that exchange, and Jachimowicz and colleagues' own bias tests on the default-only literature came out clean. The second error runs the other way. DellaVigna and Linos compared 126 nudge-unit trials covering 23 million people with nudge trials in academic journals: 8.7 percentage points and a 33.5 percent lift over control in the journals, 1.4 percentage points and 8.1 percent in the nudge units. Correcting for selective publication, with insignificant trials written up at an estimated probability of 0.1, brings the journal figure to 3.2 percentage points. Those numbers describe nudges in general, and defaults were removed from both samples. The third error is reading an acceptance rate as an effect. Eighty percent staying with a green default is a level, and the effect is the difference from what people choose with no default or the opposite one. The fourth is treating a moved choice as moved welfare, which is what Choukhmane's medium-run results deny.
